facets.label: Rhythm, meter and tempo
facets.summary: This facet covers the organization, perceived movement, and speed of musical time, including beat grouping, rhythmic relationships, and changes in pace.
facets.article:
Rhythm concerns when musical events happen and how their durations and accents relate. Meter provides a recurring framework for grouping beats, while tempo describes their rate. These dimensions interact, but they are distinct: the same rhythm can be performed at different speeds, and a steady tempo can support several patterns of accent. Listeners may perceive a pulse even when no instrument explicitly marks every beat.

The facet has four main branches. *Meter* includes regular beat groupings, changing meters, and overlapping metrical frameworks. *Rhythmic feel* describes how musicians shape the movement of a passage, including straight, swung, half-time, and laid-back approaches. *Rhythmic devices* covers relationships such as syncopation, polyrhythm, and rhythmic displacement. *Tempo* includes broad speed descriptions and ways of changing or stretching the pace.

These features help distinguish musical traditions without defining them alone. Waltzes commonly organize movement around three beats, much rock emphasizes a regular pulse with prominent backbeats, and some West African ensemble traditions combine contrasting rhythmic layers. This facet describes the temporal principles behind such differences. Specific drum grooves and percussion executions belong in *Drums and percussion patterns*; the organization of sections belongs in *Form and structure*. A genre can contain several meters, feels, or tempos.

facets.label: Drums and percussion patterns
facets.summary: This facet covers recurring drum and percussion grooves, along with playing techniques that shape their accents, textures, and rhythmic impact.
facets.article:
Drums and percussion give rhythm a particular physical and sonic form. A pattern distributes strikes, rests, and accents among instruments or playing surfaces. Its identity depends on more than the placement of beats: differences in touch, sound, timing, and interaction can make similar patterns feel substantially different. Percussion can establish a steady foundation, answer a melody, mark transitions, or become the main musical focus.

The facet is organized into *Drum patterns* and *Drum techniques*. Patterns include recognizable grooves such as four-on-the-floor, dembow, one-drop, and breakbeat-based approaches. Techniques describe how those patterns are performed or embellished, including ghost notes, rolls, flams, fills, brush playing, and linear drumming. A technique can appear within many patterns, while a pattern can be realized with acoustic instruments, electronic drums, or samples.

Percussion is often a strong clue to genre. Reggae one-drop patterns organize emphasis differently from the continuous kick pulse common in much house music. Samba ensembles distribute rhythmic roles across several percussion instruments, creating a collective groove. These examples also show why an isolated pattern cannot identify every recording reliably. General concepts such as meter, syncopation, and tempo belong in *Rhythm, meter and tempo*. Instrument identities belong in *Instrumentation*, while processing and editing percussion sounds belong in *Production and sound*.

facets.label: Harmony and tonality
facets.summary: This facet covers simultaneous pitch relationships, tonal organization, chord movement, musical closure, and changes between tonal centers.
facets.article:
Harmony concerns how pitches sound together and how those combinations relate over time. Tonality describes an organization in which a particular pitch or chord acts as a center of reference. Music can establish that center strongly, move between centers, combine several, or avoid a clear tonal center. Harmonic tension and resolution depend on musical context and learned expectations; they are not universal measures of emotional meaning.

The facet has six main branches. *Tonality* describes broad systems of pitch organization. *Chords* identifies simultaneous pitch combinations. *Harmonic devices* covers resources such as pedal points, borrowed chords, and reharmonization. *Chord progressions* describes recurring sequences, while *Cadences* concerns gestures of arrival or closure. *Modulation* covers movement between tonal centers. These branches connect individual sonorities with the larger direction of a piece.

Harmony helps distinguish styles through customary resources and their use. Western classical repertories often organize phrases around tonal movement and cadences. Jazz frequently develops extended chords and reharmonization, while blues makes distinctive use of recurring harmonic patterns. These are tendencies rather than requirements for every piece. Pitch collections considered as scales or modes belong in *Scales and modes*. The movement of a melodic line belongs in *Melody and motif*, and the interaction of simultaneous parts belongs in *Texture and counterpoint*.

facets.label: Scales and modes
facets.summary: This facet covers pitch collections and modal frameworks used to organize melodies, harmonies, and characteristic musical relationships.
facets.article:
Scales provide ways of arranging pitches, often presented in ascending or descending order. Modes describe pitch organization through relationships to a center and characteristic degrees or intervals. A collection of notes does not determine how music will sound by itself: emphasis, melodic movement, tuning, ornamentation, and harmonic context all affect its identity. Two pieces using similar pitch material can therefore have very different characters.

The facet is organized into *Scales*, *Modes*, and *Modal and tuning systems*. The first two branches include major and minor resources, pentatonic collections, symmetrical scales, named modes, and scales such as the Phrygian dominant that are shared by several traditions. The third holds frameworks that go beyond a list of pitches. Maqam and raga, for example, also involve hierarchies of degrees, characteristic phrases, ornamentation, and intonation, while the gamelan tunings pelog and slendro are properties of a particular ensemble's instruments.

Pitch frameworks help describe differences among traditions. Major and minor resources are widespread in Western tonal music; pentatonic collections occur in many musical cultures; Indian classical performance develops melodies within raga frameworks. None of these resources belongs exclusively to one genre. This facet describes the pitch material and its organizing framework. Chord function and tonal movement belong in *Harmony and tonality*, while the actual shaping, ornamentation, and development of melodic lines belong in *Melody and motif*.

facets.label: Melody and motif
facets.summary: This facet covers recognizable musical lines, recurring melodic ideas, ways of transforming or decorating them, and practices of improvisation.
facets.article:
A melody is a sequence of pitches and durations heard as a connected line. It may be sung, played by an instrument, or distributed among several performers. A motif is a shorter idea that can recur or develop within a piece. Melodic identity depends on rhythm and phrasing as well as pitch, so changing an idea’s timing can alter its character even when its notes remain similar.

The facet has three main branches. *Melodic elements* includes hooks, riffs, motifs, ostinatos, countermelodies, and other recognizable materials. *Melodic devices* describes ways of shaping a line, including sequences, chromatic movement, ornaments, and different relationships between successive notes. *Improvisation* concerns the creation or development of musical material during performance, including practices that respond to an established harmonic or modal framework.

Melodic practices help distinguish traditions and styles. A rock riff can supply a recurring instrumental identity, a jazz solo can develop ideas through improvisation, and Indian classical performance can explore characteristic melodic movements within a raga. The significance of each example lies in how material is used, rather than in the presence of melody alone. Scales and modal frameworks belong in *Scales and modes*. Vocal production belongs in *Voice and vocal technique*, while the placement of melodic ideas across a whole piece belongs in *Form and structure*.

facets.label: Form and structure
facets.summary: This facet covers the arrangement of musical sections, patterns of repetition and contrast, and established frameworks for complete compositions.
facets.article:
Form describes how a piece unfolds over time. Listeners recognize beginnings, returns, contrasts, transitions, and endings through changes in melody, harmony, rhythm, texture, or sound. A structure may follow a familiar pattern or emerge through gradual development. Understanding form helps explain why a passage feels like preparation, arrival, interruption, or return, even when the listener cannot name the sections involved.

The facet is organized into *Song sections*, *Song forms*, and *Compositional forms*. Song sections identify parts such as verses, choruses, bridges, introductions, breakdowns, and outros. Song forms describe how such parts are arranged and repeated, including verse–chorus and strophic designs. Compositional forms cover broader established frameworks and types of composition, including fugues, rondos, suites, concertos, and other resources used across different repertories.

Formal habits can provide clues to genre. Many popular songs alternate verses and choruses; some electronic dance arrangements organize anticipation around build-ups and drops; Western classical works may use recurring themes within a rondo or a larger sonata framework. Individual works can adapt or combine these practices. This facet concerns the placement and relationship of musical material across time. The material itself belongs in the relevant melodic, harmonic, rhythmic, or textural facet. Recording effects that create a transition belong in *Production and sound*, even when their structural role is described here.

facets.label: Texture and counterpoint
facets.summary: This facet covers how simultaneous musical parts combine, interact, and distribute melodic or accompanying roles.
facets.article:
Texture describes the overall relationship among musical parts sounding at the same time. Music may present one line, several closely coordinated parts, independent lines, or multiple versions of a shared melody. Texture also concerns density and the distribution of attention: a few widely spaced sounds can feel different from many overlapping parts. The number of instruments alone does not determine the texture.

The facet has three main branches. *Texture* includes broad configurations such as monophony, homophony, polyphony, and heterophony, alongside descriptions of density. *Counterpoint* concerns the interaction of distinct lines, including imitation and voice leading. *Accompaniment textures* describes ways of supporting or responding to a principal part, such as comping, drones, repeated figures, call and response, and antiphonal exchange.

Textural habits can help distinguish musical traditions. Western choral hymns may coordinate voices in chordal movement. Jazz accompaniment can leave space around an improvised lead while contributing its own rhythmic and harmonic activity. Some Indonesian gamelan repertories combine interlocking and layered parts. Such relationships may change within a single piece. This facet describes what the parts do together. Their instrument identities belong in *Instrumentation*, their pitch combinations in *Harmony and tonality*, and their individual melodic ideas in *Melody and motif*. Studio layering belongs here when describing the resulting musical relationship, and in *Production and sound* when describing the recording process.

facets.label: Voice and vocal technique
facets.summary: This facet covers singing and spoken vocal sounds, voice categories, expressive delivery, and the organization of vocal parts.
facets.article:
The human voice can carry melody, rhythm, language, and expressive character at the same time. Vocal sound depends on how a performer coordinates production, resonance, articulation, and phrasing. Descriptions such as breathy, clean, shouted, or melismatic identify different aspects of delivery rather than fixed categories of singer. A performer may use several approaches within one song, and vocal terminology varies among musical traditions.

The facet is organized into five main branches. *Voice types* describes categories based on range, timbre, or performance role. *Singing techniques* covers approaches such as falsetto, belting, vibrato, and overtone singing. *Harsh vocals* groups deliberately rough or distorted vocal timbres. *Spoken and rapped vocals* concerns speech-centered and rhythmically organized delivery. *Vocal arrangement* describes the relationship among lead voices, backing parts, harmonies, and groups.

Vocal practices are often useful clues to style. Opera commonly emphasizes sustained, projected singing; many R&B performances use melismatic ornamentation; rap foregrounds the rhythmic placement and articulation of words. These practices also travel across genre boundaries. This facet describes vocal delivery and the organization of voices, rather than the literary content of the words, which belongs in *Lyrics and prosody*. Electronic pitch correction, vocoding, and recorded vocal distortion belong in *Production and sound* when the focus is the processing method. Melodic shapes shared with instrumental music belong in *Melody and motif*.

facets.label: Instrumentation
facets.summary: This facet covers the instruments, sound-producing resources, and ensembles used to perform or construct music.
facets.article:
Instrumentation describes which sound-producing resources take part in music. These may include acoustic instruments, electronic devices, percussion, or established ensembles. Instruments contribute characteristic ranges, attacks, resonances, and possibilities of expression, but their identities do not prescribe a single musical role. A guitar can provide melody, chords, bass movement, or percussion-like gestures, and electronic instruments can imitate familiar sounds or produce unfamiliar ones.

The facet is organized into *Plucked strings*, *Bowed strings*, *Woodwinds*, *Brass*, *Keyboards*, *Electronic instruments*, *Percussion*, and *Ensembles*. These branches provide practical routes through instrument families and performance groupings. They are browsing categories rather than one universal scientific classification: keyboard instruments, for example, produce sound through several different mechanisms. Electronic resources also include recognizable devices and sounds associated with particular production practices.

Instrument combinations can strongly suggest a tradition. A string quartet identifies a familiar Western chamber ensemble; mariachi often combines strings with trumpets; Indonesian gamelan ensembles prominently use tuned percussion. Similar instruments may nevertheless appear in very different genres, and substitutions can preserve a musical role while changing its sound. This facet identifies the resources involved. How performers play them belongs in *Instrumental techniques*, the relationship among their parts in *Texture and counterpoint*, and recording or processing choices in *Production and sound*. Vocal delivery is developed separately in *Voice and vocal technique*.

facets.label: Instrumental techniques
facets.summary: This facet covers ways of playing and manipulating instruments that shape articulation, pitch, rhythm, timbre, and musical expression.
facets.article:
Instrumental technique describes the actions through which a performer produces and shapes sound. Different gestures can change a note’s attack, duration, pitch, resonance, or rhythmic emphasis. Techniques may be associated with a particular instrument, but related musical effects can arise through different physical methods. A connected phrase, for example, requires different actions on a guitar, a bowed string instrument, and a wind instrument.

The facet is organized into *Guitar techniques*, *Bass techniques*, *Keyboard techniques*, *Bowed-string techniques*, *Wind techniques*, and *DJ techniques*. These branches include picking and muting approaches, bass articulation, keyboard accompaniment patterns, bowing and plucking gestures, breath-related effects, and the manipulation of recorded material through turntables. Some entries describe recurring performance approaches, while others identify a particular gesture or sound-producing method.

Techniques help give genres their recognizable detail. Flamenco guitar makes distinctive use of strumming and plucking approaches such as rasgueado and picado. Jazz bass often supplies motion through walking lines. Hip-hop turntablism uses scratching and related manipulation as musical performance. These resources can be adopted outside their customary settings. This facet focuses on performance methods. Instrument identities belong in *Instrumentation*, broadly applicable articulations belong in *Dynamics and articulation*, and audio processing such as compression, filtering, or reverberation belongs in *Production and sound*. A processed sound may combine contributions from both playing technique and studio treatment.

facets.label: Production and sound
facets.summary: This facet covers recording choices, audio processing, sampling, sound design, and production aesthetics that shape the audible character of music.
facets.article:
Production shapes how performed or constructed sounds become a recording or amplified presentation. Decisions about capture, editing, processing, balance, and space can change the listener’s experience substantially. Production may preserve the impression of an immediate performance or create a sound that could not arise from an unprocessed ensemble. Its contribution is audible even when listeners cannot identify the equipment or methods involved.

The facet organizes these choices through several branches. *Recording aesthetic* and *Era aesthetic* describe broad sonic approaches and historical references. *Dynamics processing* concerns signal-level control, while *Spatial effects* creates or modifies perceived space. *Modulation effects*, *Distortion*, *Filters*, and *Pitch effects* alter different properties of sound. *Time manipulation* changes timing, duration, or playback direction. *Sampling* reuses recorded material, and *Sound design* develops sounds for particular musical roles.

Production practices can help distinguish styles. Dub frequently gives echo and reverberation an active musical role. Some punk recordings emphasize a direct, relatively rough presentation. Contemporary pop often uses detailed editing and layered vocal production. These are tendencies, and recordings within each tradition can differ widely.

This facet concerns how sound is captured, transformed, and presented. The performer’s physical actions belong in *Instrumental techniques* or *Voice and vocal technique*. Musical loudness and articulation as expressive performance choices belong in *Dynamics and articulation*. Historical sound labels describe selected production traits rather than everything recorded during a particular decade.

facets.label: Dynamics and articulation
facets.summary: This facet covers expressive changes in musical intensity and the ways notes are attacked, sustained, connected, or separated.
facets.article:
Dynamics concerns the relative strength or intensity of musical events. Articulation concerns how notes begin, continue, and end, including their connection or separation. Together, they shape phrasing and emphasis: the same sequence of pitches can sound restrained, forceful, flowing, or sharply marked depending on its execution. Their effects depend on musical context, instrument, and the contrasts established within a passage.

The facet has two main branches. *Dynamics* includes quiet and loud performance, gradual increases and decreases, sudden emphasis, and contrasts between passages. *Articulation* includes approaches such as staccato, legato, marcato, and tenuto. These terms describe relationships within the music rather than fixed acoustic measurements. A quiet passage can remain intense, while a strong attack need not produce a long or sustained sound.

Expressive handling helps distinguish performances and styles. Western classical repertories often use carefully shaped dynamic contrasts and articulation. Jazz phrasing can depend on subtle accents and differences in note length. Rock arrangements may create dramatic contrast between restrained verses and forceful choruses. No single pattern defines all examples of a genre. This facet describes musical expression through intensity and note shaping. Compression and limiting belong in *Production and sound* as signal-processing methods. Instrument-specific ways of achieving an articulation belong in *Instrumental techniques*, and emotional interpretations of the result belong in *Mood and character*.

facets.label: Lyrics and prosody
facets.summary: This facet covers the verbal construction of songs, including rhyme, sound patterns, narrative devices, and the relationship between words and musical delivery.
facets.article:
Lyrics contribute language, imagery, narrative, and verbal sound to music. Prosody concerns how features such as syllables, stress, rhythm, and phrasing interact with musical delivery. Words can align closely with musical accents or create expressive tension against them. Their meaning also changes through repetition, placement, and performance, so a lyric’s musical effect cannot be understood from its written text alone.

The facet is organized around *Lyrical devices*. This branch includes rhyme schemes, internal and multisyllabic rhyme, assonance, repetition, storytelling, wordplay, vocables, and other ways of shaping verbal material. It also includes broad approaches to lyrical content, such as protest, confession, and abstraction. These entries describe resources that can coexist: a narrative song can use repeated phrases, intricate rhyme, and ambiguous imagery at the same time.

Lyrical practices help distinguish traditions and individual styles. Rap often gives particular prominence to rhyme placement and verbal rhythm. Folk ballads frequently organize words around a developing story. Some flamenco singing stretches or repeats words for expressive emphasis. These practices are shared and adapted across genres. This facet concerns the words and their organization in music. Vocal timbre and delivery belong in *Voice and vocal technique*, while melodic ornamentation belongs in *Melody and motif*. The facet also records the absence of words: *Instrumental* marks pieces without sung or spoken lyrics.

facets.label: Mood and character
facets.summary: This facet covers the perceived emotional and expressive qualities of music, including atmosphere, energy, intimacy, tension, and dramatic character.
facets.article:
Mood and character describe how music is experienced rather than a single measurable feature of its construction. Listeners may hear a passage as playful, ominous, contemplative, triumphant, or intimate because of interacting musical cues and personal associations. Rhythm, timbre, register, harmony, dynamics, and words can all contribute. Interpretations also depend on cultural familiarity, listening circumstances, and what has happened earlier in the piece.

The facet is organized under *Mood*. Its concepts provide a vocabulary for broad expressive impressions, including uplifting, melancholic, aggressive, dreamy, mysterious, and spiritual qualities. Several descriptions can apply simultaneously or to different moments of one recording. A piece may combine energetic movement with dark timbres, or a restrained performance with strong emotional intensity. These terms therefore support description without imposing a single emotional identity.

Character can help compare genres, but its value depends on context. Listeners may hear playful energy in funk, solemnity in a devotional chant, or grandeur in an orchestral passage. None of these impressions belongs exclusively to that tradition. This facet records the perceived expressive result. The rhythmic, harmonic, instrumental, and production features contributing to it belong in their respective facets. Bright timbre and a bright mood, for example, are related descriptions with different meanings. Mood labels should not be treated as automatic consequences of major or minor tonality, tempo, or instrumentation.

concepts.label: Meter
concepts.definition: The recurring organization of musical beats into groups, usually represented by a time signature and patterns of strong and weak beats.
concepts.note: Organization of beats into bars with recurring accents.

concepts.label: Simple meter
concepts.definition: A meter in which each main beat normally divides into two equal parts, as in 2/4, 3/4, or 4/4.
concepts.note: Each beat divides into two.

concepts.label: 2/4 time
concepts.definition: A time signature with two quarter-note beats per bar, often heard in marches, polkas, and other duple-meter music.
concepts.note: Two beats per bar; marches, polka, cumbia.

concepts.label: 3/4 time
concepts.definition: A time signature with three quarter-note beats per bar, commonly associated with waltzes and other triple-meter music.
concepts.note: Three beats per bar; waltz, mazurka, many folk ballads.

concepts.label: 4/4 time
concepts.definition: A time signature with four quarter-note beats per bar, widely used in popular music and also called common time.
concepts.note: The default meter of nearly all popular music.

concepts.label: Compound meter
concepts.definition: A meter in which each main beat normally divides into three equal parts, as in 6/8, 9/8, or 12/8.
concepts.note: Each beat divides into three.

concepts.label: 6/8 time
concepts.definition: A time signature usually felt as two dotted-quarter-note beats per bar, each divided into three eighth notes.
concepts.note: Two triple-divided beats; jig, Irish ballads, slow doo-wop.

concepts.label: 9/8 time
concepts.definition: A time signature containing nine eighth notes per bar, usually grouped into three beats but sometimes organized asymmetrically.
concepts.note: Three triple-divided beats, or aksak groupings (2+2+2+3).

concepts.label: 12/8 time
concepts.definition: A time signature usually felt as four dotted-quarter-note beats per bar, each divided into three eighth notes.
concepts.note: Four triple-divided beats; slow blues, soul, rock and roll ballads.

concepts.label: Odd meter
concepts.definition: A meter whose subdivisions form unequal beat groups, such as 2+3 or 2+2+3, rather than a regular duple or triple pattern.
concepts.note: Bars whose beats don't group evenly.

concepts.label: 5/4 time
concepts.definition: A time signature containing five quarter notes per bar, often grouped as three plus two or two plus three.
concepts.note: Five beats (3+2 or 2+3).

concepts.label: 5/8 time
concepts.definition: A time signature containing five eighth notes per bar, commonly grouped as two plus three or three plus two.
concepts.note: Five eighth notes, grouped 2+3 or 3+2.

concepts.label: 7/8 time
concepts.definition: A time signature containing seven eighth notes per bar, commonly arranged in unequal groups such as 2+2+3.
concepts.note: Seven eighth notes (2+2+3, 3+2+2…); prog rock, Balkan music.

concepts.label: 7/4 time
concepts.definition: A time signature containing seven quarter notes per bar, often grouped into smaller units such as four plus three.
concepts.note: Seven quarter notes per bar.

concepts.label: 11/8 time
concepts.definition: A time signature containing eleven eighth notes per bar, typically organized into unequal groups of two and three.
concepts.note: Eleven eighth notes; Balkan folk, progressive metal.

concepts.label: 13/8 time
concepts.definition: A time signature containing thirteen eighth notes per bar, typically organized into an asymmetrical sequence of smaller beat groups.
concepts.note: Thirteen eighth notes; prog rock and math rock.

concepts.label: Aksak rhythm
concepts.definition: An asymmetrical rhythmic organization built from unequal short and long beat units, particularly associated with Turkish and Balkan traditions.
concepts.note: Uneven groupings of 2s and 3s typical of Turkey and the Balkans.

concepts.label: Mixed meter
concepts.definition: The use of changing time signatures within a piece or passage, producing successive bars with different beat groupings.
concepts.note: Frequent alternation of different time signatures within a section.

concepts.label: Free meter
concepts.definition: Music without a consistently recurring metrical pattern; timing may instead follow melodic phrasing, text, or expressive needs.
concepts.note: Passages without a regular pulse, shaped by the phrase.

concepts.label: Hemiola
concepts.definition: A rhythmic or metrical effect in which a span normally grouped in twos is heard in threes, or vice versa, often creating a 3:2 relationship.
concepts.note: Three duple beats laid over or alternating with two triple ones (metric 3:2).

concepts.label: Polymeter
concepts.definition: The simultaneous use of different metrical groupings in separate musical parts, often over a shared underlying pulse.
concepts.note: Simultaneous layers in different meters sharing a pulse.

concepts.label: Rhythmic feel
concepts.definition: The perceived character of a rhythm, shaped by subdivision, accent, timing, and the placement of notes around the beat.
concepts.note: How the pulse is subdivided and placed, beyond the time signature.

concepts.label: Straight feel
concepts.definition: A rhythmic feel in which equal written subdivisions are performed with approximately equal durations rather than a swing pattern.
concepts.note: Even subdivisions, no swing.

concepts.label: Swing
concepts.definition: A rhythmic feel with unequal subdivisions and flexible timing, often giving paired eighth notes a long-short character.
concepts.note: Uneven (long-short) eighth notes built on a triplet.

concepts.label: Shuffle
concepts.definition: A repeated long-short subdivision pattern, commonly based on triplets and widely used in blues, boogie-woogie, and related styles.
concepts.note: A steady, pronounced swing pattern; the basis of blues and boogie.

concepts.label: Triplet feel
concepts.definition: A rhythmic feel in which the beat is regularly divided into three parts, whether all three subdivisions are sounded or not.
concepts.note: A pulse consistently subdivided into three.

concepts.label: Half-time feel
concepts.definition: A rhythmic feel that makes the music seem slower by placing major accents at half their usual rate without necessarily changing the tempo.
concepts.note: The snare lands every other beat, so the music feels half as fast.

concepts.label: Double-time feel
concepts.definition: A rhythmic feel that makes the music seem faster by doubling the rate of prominent subdivisions or accents without necessarily changing the tempo.
concepts.note: Percussion doubles the apparent speed of the pulse.

concepts.label: Laid-back feel
concepts.definition: A timing approach in which notes sit slightly behind the expected beat, creating a relaxed or spacious groove.
concepts.note: Playing slightly behind the beat for a relaxed feel.

concepts.label: Driving feel
concepts.definition: A rhythm with persistent forward momentum, created through strong pulse, repeated accents, or assertive placement of notes.
concepts.note: Playing ahead of or insistently on the beat for urgency.

concepts.label: Rhythmic devices
concepts.definition: A compositional or performance technique that shapes rhythmic organization, accent, repetition, or the relationship between musical parts.
concepts.note: Techniques that alter or enrich the basic pattern.

concepts.label: Syncopation
concepts.definition: The emphasis of normally weak beats or subdivisions, or the displacement of accents away from the expected metrical pattern.
concepts.note: Accents on weak beats or between beats.

concepts.label: Anticipation
concepts.definition: A note or chord sounded before its expected rhythmic or harmonic position, creating a sense of forward motion.
concepts.note: A note or chord that arrives before the strong beat it was expected on.

concepts.label: Offbeat
concepts.definition: A beat or subdivision outside the main metrical accents, often emphasized to create rhythmic contrast or syncopation.
concepts.note: Systematic accenting of the weak parts of the beat.

concepts.label: Backbeat
concepts.definition: A strong accent on the second and fourth beats of a four-beat bar, commonly played on the snare drum in popular music.
concepts.note: Snare accent on beats 2 and 4 of a 4/4 bar.

concepts.label: Polyrhythm
concepts.definition: The simultaneous use of contrasting rhythmic divisions, such as three evenly spaced notes against two over the same duration.
concepts.note: Two or more conflicting subdivisions at once (3:2, 4:3…).

concepts.label: Three against two
concepts.definition: A polyrhythm in which three evenly spaced events occur against two evenly spaced events within the same time span.
concepts.note: Three even notes against two in the same span.

concepts.label: Four against three
concepts.definition: A polyrhythm in which four evenly spaced events occur against three evenly spaced events within the same time span.
concepts.note: Four notes against three in the same span.

concepts.label: Cross-rhythm
concepts.definition: A sustained rhythmic relationship in which one pattern conflicts with the main beat grouping, often serving as a structural feature.
concepts.note: Sustained polyrhythm as a structural basis, typical of West African music.

concepts.label: Clave
concepts.definition: A recurring guide pattern that organizes rhythmic relationships in Afro-Cuban music, commonly expressed as five strokes across two measures.
concepts.note: Five-stroke guide pattern in Afro-Cuban music.

concepts.label: Son clave
concepts.definition: A five-stroke Afro-Cuban clave pattern with three strokes in one measure and two in the other, played in either 3-2 or 2-3 orientation.
concepts.note: Son clave in its 3-2 and 2-3 orientations.

concepts.label: Rumba clave
concepts.definition: An Afro-Cuban clave pattern related to son clave, with a different placement of the final stroke on its three-stroke side.
concepts.note: Variant with the third stroke delayed.

concepts.label: Bossa nova clave
concepts.definition: A two-measure rhythmic pattern used in some bossa nova accompaniment, related to clave but not universally required by the style.
concepts.note: Brazilian clave variant used in bossa nova.

concepts.label: Tresillo
concepts.definition: A three-attack rhythm often represented as 3+3+2 subdivisions within an eight-unit cycle, common in Afro-Latin music and popular styles.
concepts.note: 3+3+2 grouping of eighth notes, core of Afro-Latin rhythm and today's pop.

concepts.label: Habanera rhythm
concepts.definition: A characteristic four-attack rhythm, commonly represented as 3+1+2+2 subdivisions, associated with the habanera and related dance traditions.
concepts.note: Tresillo with an added note on beat two.

concepts.label: Stop-time
concepts.definition: An accompaniment pattern of isolated ensemble accents separated by silence, leaving space for a singer or soloist.
concepts.note: The band plays only isolated hits, leaving gaps for vocals or a solo.

concepts.label: Rhythmic displacement
concepts.definition: The shifting of a rhythmic figure to a different position relative to the beat while preserving its internal pattern.
concepts.note: A motif repeated shifted against the beat.

concepts.label: Metric modulation
concepts.definition: A tempo change established through a proportional relationship between rhythmic values in the old and new tempos.
concepts.note: Tempo change derived from a shared subdivision.

concepts.label: Anacrusis
concepts.definition: One or more pickup notes that precede the first strong beat of a phrase or complete measure.
concepts.note: Notes before the first downbeat of a phrase.

concepts.label: Ensemble hits
concepts.definition: Short, coordinated accents played by several instruments together to emphasize a rhythmic point or transition.
concepts.note: Accents played by the whole band together.

concepts.label: Tempo
concepts.definition: The speed of the musical pulse, usually indicated by a verbal marking or a number of beats per minute.
concepts.note: Speed of the pulse, in beats per minute.

concepts.label: Very slow tempo
concepts.definition: A very slow musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly below 60 BPM as a descriptive guide rather than a universal boundary.
concepts.note: Below ~60 BPM.

concepts.label: Slow tempo
concepts.definition: A slow musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly 60-80 BPM as a descriptive guide, with perceived speed also depending on meter and subdivision.

concepts.label: Mid tempo
concepts.definition: A moderate musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly 85-110 BPM as a descriptive guide rather than a fixed musical category.

concepts.label: Fast tempo
concepts.definition: A fast musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly 115-150 BPM as a descriptive guide, with perceived speed varying by musical context.

concepts.label: Very fast tempo
concepts.definition: A very fast musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly above 160 BPM as a descriptive guide rather than a universal boundary.
concepts.note: Above ~160 BPM.

concepts.label: Tempo change
concepts.definition: A change in the speed of the musical pulse, either gradual or sudden, within a piece or passage.
concepts.note: Tempo variation within the piece.

concepts.label: Accelerando
concepts.definition: A gradual increase in tempo, making the musical pulse progressively faster.
concepts.note: Gradual speeding up.

concepts.label: Ritardando
concepts.definition: A gradual decrease in tempo, often used to relax a phrase or prepare a musical ending.
concepts.note: Gradual slowing down, typical of endings.

concepts.label: Rubato
concepts.definition: Expressive flexibility in timing, allowing notes or phrases to stretch and compress around the underlying pulse.
concepts.note: Expressive flexibility of tempo.

concepts.label: Fermata
concepts.definition: A notation indicating that a note, chord, or rest should be held longer than its written duration.
concepts.note: A note or rest held beyond its value.

concepts.label: Tempo switch
concepts.definition: An abrupt change from one tempo to another, usually at a section boundary or other clear structural point.
concepts.note: Sudden jump to another tempo between sections.

concepts.label: Drum patterns
concepts.definition: A recurring arrangement of drum or percussion sounds that establishes a groove, rhythmic feel, or stylistic identity.
concepts.note: Drum patterns that identify styles.

concepts.label: Basic rock beat
concepts.definition: A common rock groove combining a steady cymbal subdivision with kick-drum support and snare accents on beats two and four.
concepts.note: Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, eighth-note hi-hats.

concepts.label: Four-on-the-floor
concepts.definition: A drum pattern with a kick-drum hit on every quarter-note beat in 4/4, especially common in disco, house, and dance music.
concepts.note: Kick on every beat of a 4/4 bar; disco and house.

concepts.label: Stomp and clap beat
concepts.definition: A percussion groove built from emphatic foot-stomp or kick-like sounds alternating with handclaps.
concepts.note: Heavily accented alternating kick and handclap; glam and modern folk-pop.

concepts.label: Breakbeat
concepts.definition: A drum groove derived from or resembling a percussion break, often syncopated and used as a sampled or programmed rhythmic foundation.
concepts.note: Syncopated pattern taken from funk breaks, often sampled.

concepts.label: Amen break
concepts.definition: The widely sampled drum break from the Winstons' recording of "Amen, Brother", influential in jungle, drum and bass, and other electronic styles.
concepts.note: The break from "Amen, Brother" (The Winstons), foundation of jungle and drum and bass.

concepts.label: Chopped breaks
concepts.definition: Sampled drum breaks cut into smaller fragments and rearranged to create new rhythms, accents, or rapid variations.
concepts.note: Sampled breaks rearranged at high speed.

concepts.label: 2-step beat
concepts.definition: A syncopated garage-style groove that omits some regular four-on-the-floor kick hits while retaining a strong dance pulse.
concepts.note: Syncopated pattern without a kick on every beat; UK garage.

concepts.label: Boom bap
concepts.definition: A hip-hop production and drum style emphasizing prominent kick and snare sounds, often built from sampled breaks.
concepts.note: Dry, prominent sampled kick and snare; 90s hip hop.

concepts.label: Trap beat
concepts.definition: A programmed groove typically combining deep 808-style bass, a sparse snare or clap pattern, and rapid or rolling hi-hats.
concepts.note: Sixteenth-note hi-hats with rolls, long 808, half-time snare.

concepts.label: Trap hi-hats
concepts.definition: Rapid hi-hat patterns using rolls, short subdivisions, and triplets to add movement and detail to trap-style beats.
concepts.note: Hi-hats with 32nd-note and triplet rolls.

concepts.label: Drill beat
concepts.definition: A drill-style groove often featuring displaced snare accents, syncopated hi-hats, and sliding bass, with regional variations.
concepts.note: Displaced snare, triplet hi-hats and gliding 808.

concepts.label: Dembow
concepts.definition: A repeating rhythmic pattern central to reggaeton and related styles, rooted in dancehall and characterized by a syncopated kick-and-snare relationship.
concepts.note: Quarter-note kick with a tresillo snare (3+3+2); reggaeton.

concepts.label: One drop
concepts.definition: A reggae drum pattern emphasizing the third beat of a four-beat bar while typically leaving the first beat without a kick accent.
concepts.note: Kick and snare together only on beat three; roots reggae.

concepts.label: Steppers
concepts.definition: A reggae drum pattern with a kick on each quarter-note beat, often combined with offbeat accompaniment and dub production.
concepts.note: Quarter-note kick in reggae and dub.

concepts.label: Rockers beat
concepts.definition: A reggae drum approach with more active kick patterns than one drop, supporting a steady groove and syncopated accompaniment.
concepts.note: Late-70s reggae pattern with busier kick and hi-hat.

concepts.label: D-beat
concepts.definition: A fast punk drum pattern associated with Discharge, defined by a driving, asymmetrical kick-and-snare cycle.
concepts.note: Hardcore punk pattern derived from Discharge.

concepts.label: Skank beat
concepts.definition: A fast drum pattern that alternates kick and snare accents, commonly used in punk and extreme metal.
concepts.note: Kick and snare alternating at high speed.

concepts.label: Blast beat
concepts.definition: A very rapid drum pattern combining repeated snare, kick, and cymbal strokes, commonly heard in grindcore and extreme metal.
concepts.note: Kick, snare and cymbals at maximum speed; grindcore and death/black metal.

concepts.label: Double bass drumming
concepts.definition: Drumming that uses two bass drums or a double pedal to produce rapid, repeated, or interlocking kick-drum strokes.
concepts.note: Kick played with two beaters in continuous sixteenths or bursts.

concepts.label: Gallop rhythm
concepts.definition: A repeated rhythmic figure commonly played as an eighth note followed by two sixteenth notes, especially on guitar or bass drum.
concepts.note: Eighth–two-sixteenths figure repeated on guitar or kick; classic heavy metal.

concepts.label: Motorik
concepts.definition: A steady, repetitive 4/4 drum groove with persistent forward motion, strongly associated with krautrock.
concepts.note: Hypnotic, steady 4/4 pulse; krautrock.

concepts.label: Train beat
concepts.definition: A snare-driven groove whose repeated accents suggest the motion of a train, common in country and rockabilly.
concepts.note: Continuous snare pattern imitating a train; country and rockabilly.

concepts.label: Purdie shuffle
concepts.definition: A half-time shuffle associated with Bernard Purdie, combining a strong backbeat with shuffled subdivisions and quiet ghost notes.
concepts.note: Half-time shuffle with ghost notes.

concepts.label: Second line
concepts.definition: A New Orleans parade-derived rhythmic feel with syncopated accents, layered percussion, and a buoyant marching groove.
concepts.note: New Orleans parade groove.

concepts.label: Bossa nova beat
concepts.definition: A restrained Brazilian groove combining bass accents and syncopated upper voices or percussion, often adapted from samba accompaniment.
concepts.note: Cross-stick on the bossa clave with kick on 2.

concepts.label: Samba batucada
concepts.definition: An interlocking samba percussion groove in which low drum pulses support syncopated patterns played by higher-pitched instruments.
concepts.note: Samba percussion with surdo, caixa and tamborim.

concepts.label: Baião rhythm
concepts.definition: A northeastern Brazilian dance rhythm commonly articulated by zabumba, triangle, and other instruments in a syncopated duple groove.
concepts.note: Northeastern Brazilian rhythm with zabumba and triangle.

concepts.label: Cumbia rhythm
concepts.definition: A cumbia groove built from a repeating duple pulse and interlocking percussion patterns, with instrumentation varying by region.
concepts.note: Guacharaca or güira in eighths with kick in 2/4.

concepts.label: Tumbao
concepts.definition: A repeating syncopated accompaniment pattern, especially for bass or congas, used in Cuban music and salsa.
concepts.note: Syncopated conga or bass pattern in salsa and son.

concepts.label: Afrobeat drumming
concepts.definition: Layered, syncopated drumming that combines funk-like grooves with West African rhythmic approaches, closely associated with Afrobeat.
concepts.note: Polyrhythmic drum pattern in the style of Tony Allen.

concepts.label: Jersey club beat
concepts.definition: A fast club groove using distinctive clustered kick patterns, chopped vocals, and repeated samples associated with Jersey club.
concepts.note: Kick pattern in five-stroke bursts with bed-squeak samples.

concepts.label: Footwork beat
concepts.definition: A fast, highly syncopated electronic groove, often around 160 BPM, designed for footwork dance and rapid rhythmic interplay.
concepts.note: Syncopated kick patterns at ~160 BPM.

concepts.label: Dancehall riddim
concepts.definition: A reusable instrumental backing track or rhythmic foundation over which multiple dancehall performers can record different songs.
concepts.note: Repeated rhythm track that different artists sing over.

concepts.label: Tamborzão
concepts.definition: A percussion pattern associated with Brazilian funk carioca, combining repeated low and high drum sounds in a syncopated groove.
concepts.note: Funk carioca percussion pattern derived from Miami bass.

concepts.label: Log drum groove
concepts.definition: A rhythmic bass pattern built from the pitched, percussive log-drum sound associated with amapiano production.
concepts.note: Amapiano's percussive bass pattern.

concepts.label: Drum techniques
concepts.definition: A method of playing drums or percussion that shapes articulation, sound, coordination, or rhythmic complexity.
concepts.note: Drumming performance techniques.

concepts.label: Ghost notes
concepts.definition: Very quiet drum strokes placed between stronger accents to add movement, texture, and rhythmic nuance.
concepts.note: Very soft snare strokes between the main ones.

concepts.label: Drum fill
concepts.definition: A short drum phrase that interrupts or embellishes the main groove, often leading into a new section.
concepts.note: Short drum phrase linking sections.

concepts.label: Drum roll
concepts.definition: A rapid succession of drum strokes that creates a sustained or nearly continuous sound.
concepts.note: Rapid, continuous succession of strokes.

concepts.label: Snare build-up
concepts.definition: A repeated snare pattern that becomes denser, faster, or louder to build tension before a transition or drop.
concepts.note: Accelerating snare roll before a drop.

concepts.label: Flam
concepts.definition: A drum rudiment consisting of a soft grace stroke immediately followed by a stronger stroke, producing a thickened attack.
concepts.note: Two near-simultaneous strokes, one a grace note.

concepts.label: Cross-stick
concepts.definition: A drumming technique in which a stick rests across the drumhead and strikes the rim, producing a short, woody click.
concepts.note: Stroke with the stick resting across the rim.

concepts.label: Tribal toms
concepts.definition: A production or arrangement descriptor for repetitive tom-drum patterns with a strong percussive pulse; it does not identify a specific cultural tradition.
concepts.note: Insistent patterns on the low toms.

concepts.label: Drum solo
concepts.definition: A passage in which drums become the principal musical focus, often highlighting rhythmic invention and performance technique.
concepts.note: Showcase section for the drums.

concepts.label: Linear drumming
concepts.definition: A drumming approach in which successive notes are distributed across instruments without simultaneous strikes.
concepts.note: No two strokes coincide; fluid funk and fusion patterns.

concepts.label: Brushes
concepts.definition: A percussion technique using brushes instead of regular sticks to produce softer taps, swishes, and continuous textured sounds.
concepts.note: Playing with brushes; jazz and ballads.

concepts.label: Tonality
concepts.definition: The organization of musical pitches around a central note or chord, with relationships that create stability, motion, and resolution.
concepts.note: Organization of pitches around a tonic.

concepts.label: Major key
concepts.definition: A tonal organization centered on a major tonic chord and major-scale relationships; its expressive character depends on context.
concepts.note: Major tonal center, generally bright in character.

concepts.label: Minor key
concepts.definition: A tonal organization centered on a minor tonic chord, often drawing on natural, harmonic, and melodic minor resources.
concepts.note: Minor tonal center, generally dark in character.

concepts.label: Modality
concepts.definition: The use of a mode as a basis for melody or harmony, often without the dominant-to-tonic priorities of functional major-minor tonality.
concepts.note: Harmony based on a mode rather than major/minor functions.

concepts.label: Atonality
concepts.definition: Music that avoids establishing a stable tonal center or the conventional hierarchy of pitches found in tonal music.
concepts.note: Absence of a tonal center.

concepts.label: Polytonality
concepts.definition: The simultaneous use of two or more distinct tonal centers or keys in different musical layers.
concepts.note: Two or more keys at once.

concepts.label: Microtonality
concepts.definition: The use of pitch intervals or tuning systems that differ from the standard twelve equal divisions of the octave.
concepts.note: Intervals smaller than a semitone.

concepts.label: Chords
concepts.definition: A combination of pitches heard as a harmonic unit, sounded together or implied through successive notes.
concepts.note: Chord types by construction.

concepts.label: Triad
concepts.definition: A three-note chord consisting of a root, third, and fifth, conventionally described as major, minor, diminished, or augmented.
concepts.note: Three-note chord stacked in thirds.

concepts.label: Power chord
concepts.definition: A chord voicing built mainly from a root and perfect fifth, often doubled at the octave and lacking a third.
concepts.note: Root and fifth with no third; the basis of rock and metal.

concepts.label: Seventh chord
concepts.definition: A chord formed from a triad plus a seventh above its root, creating several common major, minor, and dominant types.
concepts.note: Triad with an added seventh.

concepts.label: Major seventh chord
concepts.definition: A chord combining a major triad with a major seventh above the root.
concepts.note: Soft-colored chord typical of jazz, soul and city pop.

concepts.label: Minor seventh chord
concepts.definition: A chord combining a minor triad with a minor seventh above the root.
concepts.note: Minor chord with a seventh; staple of R&B and neo soul.

concepts.label: Dominant seventh chord
concepts.definition: A chord combining a major triad with a minor seventh, often used to create harmonic tension or a blues color.
concepts.note: Tense chord that wants to resolve; everywhere in blues.

concepts.label: Half-diminished chord
concepts.definition: A chord combining a diminished triad with a minor seventh, also written as a minor seventh chord with a flattened fifth.
concepts.note: Diminished triad with a minor seventh.

concepts.label: Extended chords
concepts.definition: A chord that includes or implies tones beyond the seventh, such as ninths, elevenths, or thirteenths.
concepts.note: Chords with 9ths, 11ths or 13ths.

concepts.label: Suspended chord
concepts.definition: A chord in which the third is replaced by a second or fourth, producing a sound that can suggest delayed resolution.
concepts.note: The third replaced by the second or fourth.

concepts.label: Added-tone chord
concepts.definition: A chord with an added color tone, such as a second, sixth, or ninth, without necessarily including a seventh.
concepts.note: Triad with an added note but no seventh.

concepts.label: Diminished chord
concepts.definition: A chord built around a minor third and diminished fifth, sometimes extended with further minor thirds.
concepts.note: Stacked minor thirds.

concepts.label: Augmented chord
concepts.definition: A triad consisting of a root, major third, and augmented fifth, dividing the octave into equal major-third intervals.
concepts.note: Stacked major thirds.

concepts.label: Altered chord
concepts.definition: A chord containing chromatically modified tones, commonly altered fifths or ninths in dominant harmony.
concepts.note: Dominant with altered ninth or fifth.

concepts.label: Slash chord
concepts.definition: A chord symbol that specifies a bass note after a slash, which may be a chord tone or an independent added pitch.
concepts.note: Chord with a note other than the root in the bass.

concepts.label: Quartal harmony
concepts.definition: Harmony constructed mainly from stacked fourths rather than the thirds typical of triadic harmony.
concepts.note: Chords built in fourths; modal jazz.

concepts.label: Tone cluster
concepts.definition: A dense chord formed from closely adjacent pitches, often producing a compact, dissonant sound mass.
concepts.note: Adjacent notes played together.

concepts.label: Neapolitan chord
concepts.definition: A major chord built on the lowered second scale degree, commonly used in first inversion before a dominant harmony.
concepts.note: Major chord on the lowered second degree.

concepts.label: Harmonic devices
concepts.definition: A compositional technique that shapes chord relationships, harmonic color, voice leading, or tonal tension.
concepts.note: Techniques of harmonic color and motion.

concepts.label: Modal mixture
concepts.definition: The use of chords or pitches borrowed from a parallel mode, such as minor-mode harmonies within a major-key passage.
concepts.note: Chords borrowed from the parallel mode.

concepts.label: Secondary dominant
concepts.definition: A dominant-function chord that temporarily points toward a chord other than the main tonic.
concepts.note: Dominant of a degree other than the tonic.

concepts.label: Tritone substitution
concepts.definition: The replacement of a dominant seventh chord by another dominant seventh chord whose root lies a tritone away.
concepts.note: Replacing a dominant with the one a tritone away.

concepts.label: Chromatic mediant
concepts.definition: A chromatic relationship between chords or tonal centers a major or minor third apart, often involving notes outside the prevailing key.
concepts.note: Chords a third apart with a chromatic change; typical of film scores.

concepts.label: Picardy third
concepts.definition: A major tonic chord used at the end of a passage or piece otherwise set in a minor key or mode.
concepts.note: Minor-key piece ending on a major chord.

concepts.label: Tritone
concepts.definition: An interval spanning three whole tones, equivalent in equal temperament to an augmented fourth or diminished fifth.
concepts.note: Three-whole-tone interval; unsettling sound much used in metal.

concepts.label: Dissonance
concepts.definition: A relationship between pitches that creates perceived tension or instability, with its meaning depending on musical style and context.
concepts.note: Systematic use of tense, unresolved intervals.

concepts.label: Pedal point
concepts.definition: A sustained or repeated pitch that remains in one part while the surrounding harmonies change.
concepts.note: Sustained or repeated note under changing chords.

concepts.label: Reharmonization
concepts.definition: The replacement or modification of chords supporting a melody while retaining much of the melodic material.
concepts.note: Changing the chords under a known melody.

concepts.label: Harmonic rhythm
concepts.definition: The rate and pattern at which harmonies change within a musical passage.
concepts.note: Rate at which chords change.

concepts.label: Jazz harmony
concepts.definition: Harmonic practices associated with jazz, including extended chords, chromatic voice leading, substitutions, and flexible treatment of dissonance.
concepts.note: Systematic use of seventh chords, extensions and substitutions.

concepts.label: Passing chord
concepts.definition: A brief chord used to connect more stable harmonies through smooth bass movement or voice leading.
concepts.note: Brief chord connecting two structural chords.

concepts.label: Descending chromatic bass
concepts.definition: A bass line that descends through semitone steps, often supporting changing harmonies or a sustained upper structure.
concepts.note: Bass descending by semitones under changing chords.

concepts.label: Line cliché
concepts.definition: A familiar voice-leading pattern in which one note moves chromatically while much of the surrounding harmony stays fixed.
concepts.note: An inner voice moves chromatically over a fixed chord.

concepts.label: Chord progressions
concepts.definition: An ordered sequence of chords that provides harmonic movement and structure within a piece or passage.
concepts.note: Stock chord successions.

concepts.label: I–V–vi–IV progression
concepts.definition: A four-chord major-key progression moving from tonic to dominant, relative minor, and subdominant, widely used in popular music.
concepts.note: The most-used pop progression since the 2000s.

concepts.label: I–vi–IV–V progression
concepts.definition: A progression moving from tonic to relative minor, subdominant, and dominant, strongly associated with doo-wop and early popular music.
concepts.note: Progression of doo-wop and 50s pop.

concepts.label: ii–V–I
concepts.definition: A progression from the supertonic chord through the dominant to the tonic, central to much jazz harmony.
concepts.note: Basic cadential cell of jazz.

concepts.label: Twelve-bar blues
concepts.definition: A twelve-measure blues framework organized around tonic, subdominant, and dominant harmonies, with many rhythmic and harmonic variants.
concepts.note: I-IV-V scheme over twelve bars.

concepts.label: Andalusian cadence
concepts.definition: A descending four-chord pattern commonly represented as i-bVII-bVI-V in a minor-key interpretation, associated with flamenco and other styles.
concepts.note: Four-chord descent of flamenco and Spanish music.

concepts.label: Circle-of-fifths progression
concepts.definition: A chord sequence whose roots move mainly by descending fifths or ascending fourths, often creating a strong sense of harmonic direction.
concepts.note: Roots descending by fifths.

concepts.label: Pachelbel progression
concepts.definition: The eight-chord sequence associated with Pachelbel's Canon, commonly represented in major keys as I-V-vi-iii-IV-I-IV-V.
concepts.note: Eight-chord progression of the Canon in D.

concepts.label: Royal road progression
concepts.definition: A progression commonly represented as IV-V-iii-vi in a major key, associated with Japanese popular music and anime songs.
concepts.note: Signature progression of J-pop and anime.

concepts.label: i–VI–III–VII progression
concepts.definition: A minor-key four-chord loop moving i-VI-III-VII, often used for broad, dramatic effects in rock, electronic music, and soundtrack-style arrangements.
concepts.note: Minor progression of epic rock, EDM and trailers.

concepts.label: I–♭VII–IV progression
concepts.definition: A repeating I-bVII-IV chord pattern that draws on Mixolydian-scale relationships and is common in rock-oriented harmony.
concepts.note: Classic rock progression based on the Mixolydian mode.

concepts.label: Vamp
concepts.definition: A short musical phrase or chord pattern repeated for an extended period as accompaniment or a basis for improvisation.
concepts.note: Two chords alternating at length.

concepts.label: One-chord harmony
concepts.definition: A passage whose harmonic foundation remains on one chord, with interest supplied by rhythm, melody, timbre, or changing voicings.
concepts.note: Piece or section on a single chord.

concepts.label: Minor plagal cadence
concepts.definition: A movement from the minor subdominant to a major tonic, producing a characteristic borrowed-chord resolution.
concepts.note: Minor subdominant resolving to a major tonic; very emotional.

concepts.label: Cadences
concepts.definition: A melodic or harmonic gesture that marks a point of arrival, pause, or closure in a musical phrase.
concepts.note: Harmonic formulas that close a phrase.

concepts.label: Authentic cadence
concepts.definition: A cadence moving from dominant harmony to tonic harmony, with its strength depending on voicing, melody, and metric placement.
concepts.note: Dominant to tonic; conclusive close.

concepts.label: Plagal cadence
concepts.definition: A cadence moving from subdominant harmony to tonic harmony, often described as an IV-I or "Amen" close.
concepts.note: Subdominant to tonic.

concepts.label: Half cadence
concepts.definition: A phrase ending on dominant harmony, usually creating an open or expectant sense rather than full resolution.
concepts.note: Phrase ending on the dominant, left hanging.

concepts.label: Deceptive cadence
concepts.definition: A cadence in which an expected dominant-to-tonic resolution is redirected to another chord, commonly the submediant.
concepts.note: The dominant resolves to an unexpected chord.

concepts.label: Backdoor cadence
concepts.definition: A jazz-oriented resolution approaching the tonic through a dominant seventh chord on the flattened seventh scale degree, often preceded by iv.
concepts.note: Arriving at the tonic from the flat seventh.

concepts.label: Modulation
concepts.definition: A change from one tonal center or key to another within a piece or passage.
concepts.note: Change of tonal center within the piece.

concepts.label: Truck driver's modulation
concepts.definition: An abrupt upward key change, often by a semitone or whole tone near a final chorus, used to increase intensity.
concepts.note: Key change up a half or whole step in the last chorus.

concepts.label: Pivot-chord modulation
concepts.definition: A key change that uses a chord shared by the old and new keys as a connecting harmonic pivot.
concepts.note: Key change via a chord common to both keys.

concepts.label: Direct modulation
concepts.definition: A sudden change of key without a connecting pivot chord or extended harmonic preparation.
concepts.note: Key change without preparation.

concepts.label: Parallel key shift
concepts.definition: A change between major and minor keys that share the same tonic, such as C major and C minor.
concepts.note: Switching between major and minor on the same tonic.

concepts.label: Scales
concepts.definition: An ordered collection of pitches used as a basis for melody, harmony, or musical organization.
concepts.note: Ordered pitch sets used as melodic material.

concepts.label: Major scale
concepts.definition: A seven-note diatonic scale with the interval pattern whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half from its tonic.
concepts.note: Diatonic major scale.

concepts.label: Natural minor scale
concepts.definition: A seven-note scale with the interval pattern whole-half-whole-whole-half-whole-whole, equivalent to the Aeolian mode.
concepts.note: Diatonic minor scale.

concepts.label: Harmonic minor scale
concepts.definition: A minor scale with a raised seventh degree, creating a leading tone and an augmented second between the sixth and seventh degrees.
concepts.note: Minor with a raised seventh; "neoclassical" sound.

concepts.label: Melodic minor scale
concepts.definition: A minor scale conventionally using raised sixth and seventh degrees when ascending; jazz practice often retains this form in both directions.
concepts.note: Minor with raised sixth and seventh.

concepts.label: Pentatonic scale
concepts.definition: A scale containing five distinct pitches within an octave, found in many musical traditions and several different interval patterns.
concepts.note: Five-note scales.

concepts.label: Major pentatonic
concepts.definition: A five-note scale corresponding to degrees 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 of the major scale.
concepts.note: Bright pentatonic; country, folk, East Asian music.

concepts.label: Minor pentatonic
concepts.definition: A five-note scale corresponding to degrees 1, b3, 4, 5, and b7, widely used in blues and rock improvisation.
concepts.note: The basis of blues and rock solos.

concepts.label: Blues scale
concepts.definition: A scale commonly formed by adding a chromatic blue note to a pentatonic collection, with several major and minor variants.
concepts.note: Minor pentatonic with an augmented fourth (the blue note).

concepts.label: Whole-tone scale
concepts.definition: A six-note scale in which each neighboring pitch is separated by a whole tone, producing a symmetrical pitch collection.
concepts.note: Six notes a whole step apart; dreamlike effect.

concepts.label: Diminished scale
concepts.definition: An eight-note symmetrical scale alternating whole tones and semitones, also called the diminished scale in jazz contexts.
concepts.note: Alternating whole and half steps; tension in jazz, metal and film scores.

concepts.label: Chromatic scale
concepts.definition: A scale comprising all twelve semitone-separated pitch classes of the standard equal-tempered octave.
concepts.note: All twelve pitches by semitones.

concepts.label: Bebop scale
concepts.definition: An eight-note scale created by adding a chromatic passing tone to a seven-note scale, often used to align chord tones with strong beats.
concepts.note: Eight-note scale with a chromatic passing tone.

concepts.label: Altered scale
concepts.definition: A seven-note scale used over altered dominant chords, equivalent to the seventh mode of the ascending melodic minor scale.
concepts.note: Scale for altered dominants in jazz.

concepts.label: Phrygian dominant scale
concepts.definition: A scale with degrees 1, b2, 3, 4, 5, b6, b7, equivalent to the fifth mode of harmonic minor.
concepts.note: Phrygian with a major third; flamenco, klezmer and Middle Eastern music.

concepts.label: Double harmonic scale
concepts.definition: A seven-note scale with lowered second and sixth degrees relative to major, producing two augmented-second intervals.
concepts.note: Scale with two augmented seconds.

concepts.label: Hungarian minor scale
concepts.definition: A minor scale with raised fourth and seventh degrees, corresponding to 1, 2, b3, #4, 5, b6, 7.
concepts.note: Harmonic minor with an augmented fourth.

concepts.label: Japanese scales
concepts.definition: Scale resources associated with Japanese traditions, including several pentatonic patterns whose intervals and uses vary by repertory.
concepts.note: Japanese pentatonics with semitones.

concepts.label: Modes
concepts.definition: A pitch framework defined by its interval pattern and tonal center; in Western theory, modes often refer to rotations of a diatonic scale.
concepts.note: Rotations of the diatonic scale, each with its own color.

concepts.label: Dorian mode
concepts.definition: A minor-type diatonic mode with a major sixth and minor seventh, corresponding to 1, 2, b3, 4, 5, 6, b7.
concepts.note: Minor with a major sixth; funk, modal jazz, Celtic folk.

concepts.label: Phrygian mode
concepts.definition: A minor-type diatonic mode with a lowered second degree, corresponding to 1, b2, b3, 4, 5, b6, b7.
concepts.note: Minor with a minor second; flamenco and metal.

concepts.label: Lydian mode
concepts.definition: A major-type diatonic mode with a raised fourth degree, corresponding to 1, 2, 3, #4, 5, 6, 7.
concepts.note: Major with an augmented fourth; magical or floating sound, common in film scores.

concepts.label: Mixolydian mode
concepts.definition: A major-type diatonic mode with a lowered seventh degree, corresponding to 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, b7.
concepts.note: Major with a minor seventh; classic rock and folk.

concepts.label: Locrian mode
concepts.definition: A diatonic mode with a lowered second and fifth, corresponding to 1, b2, b3, 4, b5, b6, b7.
concepts.note: Mode with a diminished fifth; very unstable sound.

concepts.label: Modal and tuning systems
concepts.definition: A grouping for frameworks of particular musical traditions that organize pitch beyond a scale, through hierarchies of degrees, characteristic phrases, ornament, intonation or ensemble tuning.
concepts.note: Frameworks of particular traditions that go beyond a set of pitches: hierarchy of degrees, characteristic phrases, ornament, intonation or the tuning of an ensemble. Plain scales are under Scales.

concepts.label: Maqam
concepts.definition: A modal framework in Arabic music governing pitch relationships, melodic movement, and expression; related systems also exist in neighboring traditions.
concepts.note: Arabic and Turkish modal system with microtones.

concepts.label: Raga
concepts.definition: A melodic framework in Indian classical music defined by characteristic pitches, movements, phrases, and expressive conventions, rather than a scale alone.
concepts.note: Melodic framework of Indian classical music.

concepts.label: Gamelan tuning systems
concepts.definition: The tuning systems of Indonesian gamelan, slendro and pelog, whose interval sizes vary from one ensemble to another.
concepts.note: General term; use Pelog or Slendro when the system is known.

concepts.label: Pelog
concepts.definition: A gamelan tuning of seven tones per octave with unequal intervals, from which pieces usually draw five-tone subsets.
concepts.note: Seven-tone gamelan tuning with unequal steps; pieces usually use five-tone subsets.

concepts.label: Slendro
concepts.definition: A gamelan tuning of five tones per octave with intervals of roughly equal size.
concepts.note: Five-tone gamelan tuning with nearly equal steps.

concepts.label: Melodic elements
concepts.definition: A recognizable unit of melodic material, such as a motif, riff, or phrase, that helps shape a composition.
concepts.note: Recognizable melodic units.

concepts.label: Hook
concepts.definition: A memorable musical or lyrical idea designed to attract attention and remain recognizable after listening.
concepts.note: Short, catchy phrase designed to stick.

concepts.label: Riff
concepts.definition: A short, recurring instrumental figure that provides rhythmic, melodic, or harmonic identity to a piece.
concepts.note: Short repeated instrumental figure that carries the song.

concepts.label: Motif
concepts.definition: A brief musical idea that can be repeated, varied, or developed to help unify a composition.
concepts.note: Smallest melodic or rhythmic idea that gets developed.

concepts.label: Leitmotif
concepts.definition: A recurring musical idea associated with a character, place, object, or dramatic concept.
concepts.note: Motif tied to a character or idea that recurs.

concepts.label: Ostinato
concepts.definition: A musical pattern repeated persistently, often providing a stable foundation beneath changing material.
concepts.note: Persistently repeated figure.

concepts.label: Ground bass
concepts.definition: A short bass line repeated many times while the upper parts vary above it.
concepts.note: The repeated bass line itself; for the variation forms built on it use Passacaglia or Chaconne.

concepts.label: Countermelody
concepts.definition: A secondary melodic line that complements or contrasts with the principal melody.
concepts.note: Secondary line in dialogue with the main melody.

concepts.label: Topline
concepts.definition: The principal vocal melody, often written together with lyrics over an existing instrumental backing track.
concepts.note: Main sung melody over the track.

concepts.label: Arpeggio
concepts.definition: The notes of a chord played successively rather than simultaneously, often in an ascending or descending pattern.
concepts.note: Chord notes played one after another.

concepts.label: Melodic sequence
concepts.definition: The repetition of a melodic idea at a different pitch level, preserving much of its interval or rhythmic shape.
concepts.note: A motif repeated at other pitches.

concepts.label: Melodic devices
concepts.definition: A technique used to shape, vary, decorate, or connect melodic material.
concepts.note: Techniques of ornament and color in the line.

concepts.label: Chromaticism
concepts.definition: The use of pitches outside a prevailing diatonic scale, often involving semitone motion or altered harmonies.
concepts.note: Use of out-of-scale notes by semitones.

concepts.label: Blue note
concepts.definition: A pitch inflection associated with blues expression, often involving flexible or lowered versions of the third, fifth, or seventh scale degree.
concepts.note: Flattened, ambiguous third, fifth or seventh.

concepts.label: Ornamentation
concepts.definition: Decorative notes or gestures that embellish a melody without replacing its main structural pitches.
concepts.note: Decorative notes on the melody.

concepts.label: Trill
concepts.definition: A rapid alternation between a principal note and a nearby pitch, usually a scale step above it.
concepts.note: Rapid alternation between two neighboring notes.

concepts.label: Mordent
concepts.definition: A short ornament that moves from a principal note to a neighboring note and quickly returns.
concepts.note: Quick ornament with a neighboring note.

concepts.label: Grace note
concepts.definition: A brief ornamental note whose timing is understood in relation to an adjacent principal note rather than as a fully independent rhythmic value.
concepts.note: Brief ornamental note before the main one.

concepts.label: Acciaccatura
concepts.definition: A grace note played as quickly as possible, almost together with the main note it precedes.

concepts.label: Appoggiatura
concepts.definition: A non-chord note that falls on the beat and resolves by step to a chord note; as an ornament, it takes part of the main note's value.
concepts.note: Leaning note on the beat that resolves by step; ornamental or harmonic.

concepts.label: Turn
concepts.definition: An ornament that circles a principal pitch by visiting upper and lower neighboring notes.
concepts.note: Ornament that circles the main note.

concepts.label: Glissando
concepts.definition: A movement between pitches by sliding continuously or passing rapidly through intervening notes, depending on the instrument.
concepts.note: Slide through the pitches between two notes, continuous or as a rapid scale.

concepts.label: Portamento
concepts.definition: A smooth, continuous glide from one note to the next used as an expressive connection, as in singing, bowed strings or a synthesizer's glide setting.
concepts.note: Expressive glide that connects one note to the next; on synthesizers often called glide.

concepts.label: Melisma
concepts.definition: The singing of several notes on a single syllable of text.
concepts.note: The device; for a style of singing use Melismatic singing, for fast ornamental passages Vocal runs.

concepts.label: Syllabic setting
concepts.definition: A vocal setting in which each syllable is generally assigned one note rather than a sequence of notes.
concepts.note: One note per syllable.

concepts.label: Conjunct motion
concepts.definition: Melodic movement mainly by neighboring scale steps rather than wide intervals.
concepts.note: Melody moving by step.

concepts.label: Disjunct motion
concepts.definition: Melodic movement characterized by leaps larger than a scale step.
concepts.note: Melody with wide leaps.

concepts.label: Octave doubling
concepts.definition: The performance of the same melodic line at pitch levels one or more octaves apart.
concepts.note: Line doubled at the octave.

concepts.label: Improvisation
concepts.definition: The creation or substantial shaping of music during performance rather than following a completely fixed written part.
concepts.note: Melodic creation in real time.

concepts.label: Modal improvisation
concepts.definition: Improvisation organized around a mode or limited set of modal harmonies, allowing melodic exploration over relatively stable accompaniment.
concepts.note: Improvising over a mode with few chord changes.

concepts.label: Trading fours
concepts.definition: An improvisational exchange in which performers alternate four-measure phrases, commonly between soloists and a drummer in jazz.
concepts.note: Soloists alternating every few bars.

concepts.label: Song sections
concepts.definition: A distinct part of a song, identified by its musical material, lyrical role, or position within the arrangement.
concepts.note: Building blocks of a popular song. Many work as structure tags in prompts.

concepts.label: Intro
concepts.definition: An opening passage that establishes atmosphere, rhythm, or musical material before the main body of a piece.
concepts.note: Opening section before the first verse.

concepts.label: Verse
concepts.definition: A recurring song section whose music is often similar each time while its lyrics develop or change.
concepts.note: Narrative section with changing lyrics.

concepts.label: Pre-chorus
concepts.definition: A section between verse and chorus that prepares the chorus through rising tension, contrasting material, or transitional harmony.
concepts.note: Section that builds tension before the chorus.

concepts.label: Chorus
concepts.definition: A recurring central section of a song, usually carrying its main hook and relatively stable lyrics.
concepts.note: Central section repeated with the same lyrics.

concepts.label: Post-chorus
concepts.definition: A section immediately after the chorus that extends its energy or presents an additional hook.
concepts.note: Extra hook after the chorus.
